title: Box, Rc and RefCell
intro: A smart pointer is a value that owns data somewhere else, lets you reach it as if it were the value itself, and cleans it up when it goes out of scope. `Box<T>` is one owner on the heap. `Rc<T>` is several owners with a count. `RefCell<T>` lets you change something through a shared reference, by checking the borrowing rules when the program runs. Together they cover the cases where ownership really is shared. Most programs need them in a few places; the rest of the time a plain value or a reference does the job.

coming_from.go: Go has no owning pointer types: a `*T` is a plain pointer, and the garbage collector frees what nobody can reach. Copying a pointer is how you share, and every holder may change the value. Most Go pointers, passed to a function that uses them for the call, become a plain `&T` or `&mut T` in Rust. `Rc<T>` is for the sharing that remains, with the owners counted, and read-only until you add a `RefCell`. `Drop` does the job `defer` does, tied to the value instead of the function.
coming_from.kotlin: Every object reference is already shared, and the JVM frees an object when nothing can reach it. `Rc<T>` is that sharing as an opt-in, with a count you can read, and a value inside an `Rc` is read-only until you add a `RefCell`. `Box<T>` is the other case: one owner, no sharing.
coming_from.python: CPython frees most objects by counting references, which is what `Rc` does, but it counts every name for you and lets any name change the object. In Rust you ask for the count (`Rc`), and you ask for the right to change shared data (`RefCell`). A cycle is collected by Python's cycle collector, and is not by `Rc`. Most of what you share by passing a name to a function is a plain `&` in Rust.
coming_from.typescript: Objects are shared by reference and freed by the garbage collector, and any name may change the object. `Rc<T>` is that sharing made explicit, with a count and read-only access, and `RefCell<T>` is the way to change a shared value. `Box<T>` is the one-owner case that JavaScript has no word for.
coming_from.java: Every object variable is already a shared reference, freed by the garbage collector when unreachable. `Rc<T>` is an opt-in version with a visible count, and a value in an `Rc` is read-only until you add a `RefCell`. The JVM also reclaims reference cycles; `Rc` does not. You never need `WeakReference` to break a cycle in Java; `Weak<T>` is how you write a back-pointer that does not keep its target alive.
coming_from.csharp: A class instance is already a shared reference that the garbage collector frees when unreachable. `Rc<T>` is that sharing as an opt-in, with a count, read-only until you add a `RefCell`. `Box<T>` is the single owner; `Weak<T>` is the `WeakReference` that does not keep the value alive.
coming_from.c: In C you share a value by copying its pointer and decide by hand who calls `free`. An `Rc<T>` is that pattern with the count and the `free` written once, in the type, so the value is freed when the last owner goes. A `Box<T>` is one `malloc` with one owner, freed when it goes out of scope.
coming_from.cpp: `Box<T>` is `std::unique_ptr<T>`, but a moved-from Rust box cannot be used at all (a compile error), where a moved-from `unique_ptr` is a null pointer that you may dereference by mistake (undefined behaviour). `Arc<T>` is `std::shared_ptr<T>`, and `Rc<T>` is closest to `shared_ptr<const T>` with a count that is never atomic: the standard library offers no such pointer to ask for, and Rust makes the choice in the type. `Weak<T>` is `std::weak_ptr<T>`.

notes: A smart pointer owns data that lives elsewhere (usually the heap), derefs to it, so `*b` and `b.method()` reach the data, and runs `Drop` to free it. `Box<T>` has one owner, `Rc<T>` has several and counts them, and the value is freed when the count reaches zero.
`Rc::clone(&a)` copies a pointer and adds one to the count. It does not copy the data. `Rc::ptr_eq(&a, &b)` says whether two `Rc`s point at the same allocation.

An `Rc` gives out only shared references, because several owners may be reading. To change the value you wrap it in `RefCell<T>`, which checks the borrowing rules when the program runs: a second `borrow_mut()` while one is alive panics instead of failing to compile.

Two `Rc`s that own each other never reach zero, so neither is freed. Make one of the links a `Weak<T>`, which does not count as an owner and gives back `None` once the value is gone. `Rc` is for one thread; `Arc` is the version that threads may share.

gotcha.title: Changing a value through a shared Rc
gotcha.looks_fine: In Go, Kotlin, Java, C#, Python, TypeScript, C and C++, two names for one object may both change it, and the second change sees the first.
gotcha.rust_sees: `Rc<Counter>` hands out only shared references (`&Counter`), because any other owner may be reading the value at the same time. `a.hits += 1` needs a unique one (`&mut`), and the `Rc` has no way to give it.
gotcha.why: This is the borrowing rule from earlier lessons, applied to owners: any number of readers, or one writer. The compiler cannot know how many owners an `Rc` has, because the count changes while the program runs, so `Rc` never hands out `&mut`, even to a single owner. When you do need to change shared data, `RefCell` moves the same check to run time, as `fixed.rs` does: it allows the write when no other borrow is alive, and panics when one is.

go.says: Go runs this and prints hits: 2. Both names are the same pointer and either may change the struct. Nothing checks who else is using it.

kotlin.says: Kotlin runs this and prints hits: 2. `a` and `b` are two references to one object, and a `var` property can be changed through either.

python.says: Python prints hits: 2. `b = a` makes a second name for the same object.
python.code:
class Counter:
    def __init__(self):
        self.hits = 0


a = Counter()
b = a

a.hits += 1
b.hits += 1
print("hits:", a.hits)

typescript.says: Prints hits: 2. `a` and `b` refer to one object and either may change its field.

java.says: Java runs this and prints hits: 2. `b = a` copies the reference, not the object.

csharp.says: C# runs this and prints hits: 2. A class instance is shared by reference.

c.says: C runs this and prints hits: 2. Two pointers to one struct, with nothing to say who may write.

cpp.says: C++ runs this and prints hits: 2. A `std::shared_ptr<Counter>` counts its owners as `Rc` does and lets every owner change the value. The read-only form is `shared_ptr<const Counter>`, which is what `Rc<Counter>` is.

cycle.py.code:
import gc
import weakref


class Node:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        self.other = None

    def __del__(self):
        print("freed", self.name)


def make_cycle():
    a = Node("a")
    b = Node("b")
    a.other = b
    b.other = a
    return weakref.ref(a)  # does not keep a alive


gc.disable()  # keep the automatic cycle collector out of the way

lone = Node("lone")
del lone  # the count falls to zero: freed on the spot, like an Rc
print("after del lone")

ref = make_cycle()  # each node is still referenced by the other
print("after make_cycle: a and b not freed, weakref alive:", ref() is not None)
found = gc.collect()  # the cycle collector finds them
print("gc.collect found garbage:", found > 0)
print("weakref alive now:", ref() is not None)
